opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the most underappreciated differences between AI systems and human workers, and it could matter a great deal for how quickly things change.

Consider how a human becomes a really good doctor or lawyer. After the formal training there's a long apprenticeship of experience: thousands of cases, the odd mistake, gradually developing a feel for which patients are sicker than they look. And that experience is locked inside one person's head. When they retire, most of it goes with them. We pass some of it on through teaching and writing, but that's a very lossy, slow channel.

AI systems don't necessarily face that bottleneck. If you have a million copies of a model deployed as, say, junior analysts or medical assistants, each encountering different situations, then in principle what they learn can be pooled. The lessons from all of those interactions could be fed back into a single shared model and redistributed to every copy. So instead of each instance having one career's worth of experience, every instance could effectively draw on the combined experience of all of them. It would be as if every doctor in the world could instantly share in what every other doctor learned that week.

That could compress the timeline dramatically. One of the reasons people have felt somewhat reassured is that current systems are good at the knowledge part of a profession but weaker at the tacit, experiential part: the judgment you only get from years on the job. Pooled experience is precisely a way of acquiring that tacit layer fast. Something that takes a human a decade could take a fleet of deployed models a matter of months, or less.

I'd add a few caveats, though. First, it's not yet clear how well current techniques actually let models learn from deployment. Today most of the learning happens in training, and models don't really update from their day-to-day work in a deep way. Making that loop work well is a real technical challenge, and there are open questions about whether merging lots of separate experiences produces a coherent improvement or a muddle. Second, a lot of professional skill is in the feedback: you need to find out whether your decision was actually right, and in many fields that signal is slow, noisy, or missing. Pooling doesn't fix bad feedback. Third, there are privacy and safety issues: you don't necessarily want everything one copy saw to propagate everywhere, and you'd want to be careful about errors or bad behaviours spreading just as quickly as good ones.

But stepping back, I think the key point is this. When people forecast how fast AI will be integrated into the economy, they often implicitly imagine it moving at the pace at which humans learn and institutions adapt. Collective learning across copies is one of the mechanisms that could break that analogy, and if it works, the transition from "promising but inexperienced" to "seasoned professional" could happen much faster than our intuitions suggest. That's a reason to be thinking about the governance questions now, rather than assuming we'll have a long, gradual period to adjust.

r001.rationale: The response says lessons from many deployed AI copies could be pooled and redistributed, letting each draw on their combined experience and compressing professional learning from years to months or less.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is one of those things that I think is genuinely underappreciated when people compare AI systems to humans. When a human doctor or lawyer or engineer learns their trade, they get one lifetime's worth of experience. Maybe forty years of cases. And when they retire, almost all of that tacit knowledge just evaporates. We try to pass it on through textbooks and mentorship, but it's incredibly lossy.

Now imagine instead that you've got a million copies of the same model deployed across the world, each one encountering different patients, different clients, different edge cases, and all of that experience can be pooled back into the next version. In a single day, that collective might see more cases than any individual human sees in a career. So the rate at which the system climbs the learning curve for a profession isn't bounded by the human timescale anymore. It's bounded by how many instances you've got running and how efficiently you can consolidate what they've learned.

And I think the consequence is that the transition for a given role could be quite abrupt. You'd have a period where the model is clearly worse than an experienced practitioner, because it just hasn't seen enough of the long tail of weird situations that the senior person has. And then, because the experience accumulates in parallel rather than serially, it could go from novice to something that's seen more cases than any human alive in a matter of months rather than decades.

Now, there are some caveats. It's not obvious that pooling experience is as straightforward as it sounds. Right now the main way models improve is through retraining, and there's a lag there, and you lose some fidelity. And some professional knowledge is bound up with having a persistent relationship with a particular person or institution, which doesn't pool in the same way. But even granting all that, I think the basic asymmetry is real and it's quite profound. Humans learn one at a time and forget. These systems can learn collectively and don't have to. That alone would make me expect the diffusion of AI into skilled professions to be faster and more sudden than historical analogies with previous technologies would suggest.

r001.rationale: The response explains that many deployed model instances can pool experience in parallel, helping a system accumulate professional cases and progress from novice to expert much faster.

astra-6.text:
Well, humans have a fairly severe bottleneck here: each of us has to learn from our own experience. If you want to become a really good doctor, you spend years seeing patients, making decisions, and finding out what happened. You can learn from other doctors, of course, but you can’t simply acquire all of their experience.

With AI, it may be possible for many copies of a model to work on different cases and then pool what they’ve learned. So instead of one doctor accumulating a year of experience in a year, you could have thousands of copies collectively accumulating thousands of years of experience, and use that to improve the model that they all share.

That doesn’t mean you automatically get thousands of times faster progress. Some outcomes take time to observe, and learning from experience requires good feedback. But it does suggest that the time it takes a human to master a profession could be a very misleading guide to how long it would take an AI. Once it can learn effectively on the job, it might move from being a novice to being extremely capable surprisingly quickly.

r001.rationale: The candidate says many copies of an AI model could work on different cases, pool what they learn, and collectively gain experience much faster, accelerating improvement in professional roles such as medicine.

sol-6.1.text:
One of the striking things is that AI systems could pool their experience in a way that humans can’t. If you want to become a doctor, you have to spend years seeing patients and learning from those cases. You can learn from other doctors, of course, but you can’t simply acquire all of their experience.

With AI, you could have thousands of copies of a model doing different instances of the same job, and then use what they’ve all learned to improve the shared model. So a year of experience across those copies could potentially amount to thousands of years of practice feeding into one system.

That doesn’t mean it automatically becomes an excellent doctor. There are questions about how well the learning transfers, whether it gets good feedback, and whether it learns the right lessons. But it does suggest that judging its learning speed by how long one human takes to master a profession could be very misleading.

r001.rationale: It says many copies can work on different instances of the same job and feed their combined learning into a shared model, potentially turning one year of experience into thousands of years of practice.
